Sir, my question is the following: In July of 1995, did you learn any information or hear any rumors about a coded telegram which would have been received at the 2nd Battalion command on the night of 14 to 15 July, but specifically a telegram ordering the 2nd Battalion to provide soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I heard rumors about a conversation between the commander and the brigade commander, a conversation about some men that they were looking after, but I don't know when this -- what this was all about. But this was sometime after July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But a telegram in July 1995 asking or ordering the 2nd Battalion to provide men to execute prisoners of war, you never heard about that in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that I ever heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, maybe it's a translation. It says here "I cannot confirm I ever heard ..." I just want to suggest to you, you never heard about such a telegram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard of such a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, how well did you know Milisav Cvijetinovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him rather well. We served in the same service for several years, certainly for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, when he testified - and I quote from page 25836 to 25837 - he said the following, I'll just quote a small part: "Q. And during the same period, did you hear any rumors about a telegram being received by the 2nd Battalion asking for soldiers to participate in the execution of prisoners?" His answer, on line 23, was: "No." Sir, my question is the following: Based on your knowledge of the character and personality of Cvijetinovic, if he knew any information about such a telegram in July 1995, do you believe he would have had the guts to speak the truth about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It calls for speculation, Your Honour. I frankly don't see the relevance of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to your next question, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness was the commander of the section, he knows the man, he can say if he believes the man spoke the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I move to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move, sir, to a different part of my cross-examination dealing with communications between the 2nd Battalion and the Zvornik Brigade. You can confirm, sir, the existence of an induction phone line between the 2nd Battalion and the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we say "induction phone," first the line goes through the communications centre of the 2nd Battalion and then to the battalion command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a switchboard in the battalion, and there is one in the brigade. A switchboard means that every participant in the battalion is connected to the battalion's switchboard. And every participant in the brigade is connected to the brigade switchboard. And between the brigade and the battalion, there is the encircled induction line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can confirm that when we say "induction phone," this is a line which is actually a link by a hardwire, and this wire is either buried or hidden and it goes into friendly territory only; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not hidden. However, it is within our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, you would agree it is placed so that -- to at least avoid the line from being broken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So linesmen sometimes would bury the line and sometimes would put the lines in the trees. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not bury the line in the ground. We just stretch it through the branches of the trees and towards the brigade. We used the official postal line without any signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, the only way communication by an induction phone can be intercepted, you will agree with me, is by plugging into the wire, in other words, by bugging the phone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is as much as I know, unless there is something more state-of-the-art.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when Sreten Acimovic testified, and that was on page 13071-13072, he was asked: "This was a secure line, meaning that conversations on such a telephone cannot be intercepted unless you plug yourself in the wire." And his answer was: "Yes." And a little later at line 22, he was asked: "So these conversations cannot be intercepted once again unless someone plugs right into the wire." And his answer was: "Yes." So subject to what you just mentioned, you agree that this is a secure line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for this reason, when you used the military induction phone, whether between the battalion command and the companies or between the battalion command and the brigade, there was no reason to use codes. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, according to what you said to the Prosecution, there was also a normal civilian phone line between the Zvornik Brigade and the 2nd Battalion command. Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 2nd Battalion had a civilian telephone line. It could dial anybody in Holland, for example, or anywhere else, anyone who had a civilian telephone line; not only the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you -- are you sure that this telephone line was operational in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. The switchboard, I believe, was in Petkovci or in Sekovici. I don't know anything about the quality of the line. It varied from one day to the next. It all depended on how good the maintenance people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that in fact this line was regularly down and not operational. Is that something you can confirm?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. What do you mean "not operational"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with me that during the war, and more specifically in July 1995, there were many days when the civilian phone line was not working, simply because civilian phones were not working. Do you recall this when you were there in your own experience?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It did happen that sometimes it worked and sometimes it didn't, but I don't know when those things happened. That telephone line was not within my range, so I wouldn't know when it worked or when it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the civilian phone in the 2nd Battalion command is not linked in any way to the communications centre where you work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, unless the brigade was first dialed, and then the brigade would transfer the call to the communications centre which would have been kind of stupid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you can confirm that a civilian line, the one you are talking about, is really a normal civilian phone using PTT assets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that such a civilian line as between the 2nd Battalion command and the Zvornik Brigade also goes through hardwire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one way to intercept such communication on a civilian phone line is basically to tap the line, in other words, bugging the phone. That's one way you could do it? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know in which way a line can be intercepted. I don't have any knowledge of that. I don't have any expertise in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you're not aware in July of 1995 of any existing technical capability that will allow you to tap into a civilian line; it's not something you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, you will agree with me that when people spoke using on that civilian phone between the battalion command and the brigade, they spoke in clear language and no codes were used. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that since the communications centre was 100 metres away from the command. I wasn't able to know how anyone spoke. Of course, when one uses a civilian phone line, one engages in normal conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you will agree with me that radio communications is entirely different from having a conversation either on the induction phone or on the civilian line because radio signals can easily be intercepted simply by using another radio and a frequency scanner. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So there is a reason when communicating by radio to use codes if you want to keep the content of your conversation confidential. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Whether there is a reason for something or not, I don't know. But I suppose if something is important, it probably needs encoding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the 2nd Battalion command, there was a RUP-12 radio in the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But there was no RUP-12 radio in the battalion command itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was one in the communications centre, but none in the command of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So any information coming to the 2nd Battalion via radio would first be received by the signalman on duty in the communications centre, and then this information would be transmitted to the battalion command using the military induction phone. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that other than for radio checks, the RUP-12 was almost never used while you were a member of the 2nd Battalion command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the communications centre, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the reason for this is quite simple. It's much easier to use the induction phone because you can speak in clear without using codes. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one more question about codes. You will agree with me that the object and purpose of using codes or coded language in wartime is to avoid the enemy from intercepting your communications. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And based on the information you provided to the Prosecution, I take it you can confirm that you, yourself, you can only recall three times where codes were used during the period you were a member of the 2nd Battalion command. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were used in November and December of 1993 during active combat activities and in April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the only other time you recall codes ever being used was when you say a coded telegram would have been received at the 2nd Battalion command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to use them, but I wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your answer. Do you recall while you were a member of the 2nd Battalion whether codes were ever used other than for the occasions you had just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Codes were not used. The Razgovornik was not used. And as for the code table, we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like now to quickly go through the manner in which the coded telegram you say was received by the 2nd Battalion, so the manner in which it was received and who actually received it. So in your interview, you stated that one night before 13 July, 1995, as you establish, you were called by Mitar Lazarevic and you were asked to come to the battalion command with the Razgovornik to decode a telegram which had arrived. Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you were called by Mitar Lazarevic that night to go to the 2nd Battalion command, the telegram you were asked to decode had already arrived and was in possession of Mitar Lazarevic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the moment you were called to go to the battalion command, you were then in the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were there any other communicators or signalmen present with you that night at the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be certain, but I believe it was Ilic. Somebody had to stay behind and operate the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this coded telegram which would have been received, you did not receive this telegram yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you showed up at the command, they gave it to you on paper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Mitar Lazarevic, according to what you said to the Prosecution, he did not tell you specifically how this telegram was received, did he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it's possible that this telegram could have been delivered by courier and you don't know that. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was possible? Well, several things were possible, and I can't claim with any certainty that one or the other was correct. I don't remember receiving it. But it was, of course, possible that a courier had brought it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to address now what happened when you arrive at the battalion command that night and before 13 July, 1995, as you say, when the telegram would have been received. Do you agree that Mitar Lazarevic called you specifically for the purpose of decoding a telegram he had received?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you went to the 2nd Battalion command alone. No other communicators went there with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you entered the battalion command, you were given the coded telegram on a sheet of paper A4.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you never saw a coded telegram written in any book. All you were given was a sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And there was another person there beside Mitar Lazarevic, but according to what you said to the Prosecution, you don't remember who that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, according to your interview, there were only the three of you in the battalion command at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you tried to decode the telegram, but you were not able to, as you said, using the Razgovornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, to the best of your knowledge, the Razgovornik you had was up to date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "up to date;" that it was in use?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was it the latest version that you had received from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a valid one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But when my colleague asked you the question whether you knew who was responsible to receive this Razgovornik, it could have been anyone in your section who received the latest version of the Razgovornik.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when Mitar Lazarevic saw that you were not able to decode that message, did you tell him the reason why you could not decode the telegram was because you needed another code book in addition to the Razgovornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not how I explained it to him. I explained it to him the following way: That one could not decipher the text with the help of the Razgovornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Mitar Lazarevic tell you, Well, there is a copy on the wall of the code book which is required that you need to decipher the message?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about the third person? Did he tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't recall him saying anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would I be right in saying that to your knowledge, and that of Mitar Lazarevic and the other person present that night, that the 2nd Battalion did not have the necessary code book required to decode the type of telegram which had been received?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try to be more precise. Based on everything you said so far how things happened, while you are there with Mitar Lazarevic and the third person, the three of you don't know of any other deciphering table available other than the Razgovornik that you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that, and I don't know if they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that if they did, they would have pointed to you, that they would have shown you that -- that thing on the wall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, after you establish clearly that you could not decode that telegram, one of the two persons there decided to wake up the commander, Acimovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then when he arrived, that is Acimovic, he was given the sheet of paper on which there was a coded telegram transcribed on it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this telegram was not decoded, of course, when it was given to Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not decoded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if Mitar Lazarevic testified that the coded telegram he received on 14 July was decoded by a signalman, of course it cannot be the same telegram that you could not decode?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that statement or about that other telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll try to be more clear. He testified about the telegram he says he received on 14 July, and he said the signalman decoded the telegram. So given that you could not decode that telegram, of course we are not talking about the same telegram. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: If that's what he said, I agree. I wasn't able to decode it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when Acimovic testified about the 14 July telegram he says he received, he said you showed up to the battalion command and the telegram was already decoded. So again it can't be the same telegram that you are talking about. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can only agree with what I know about it and that's that I could not decode it. I don't know what happened to them that same night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, coming back to the telegram that you are aware of. Sreten Acimovic did not ask you to stay and to decode that message using the table he pointed to on the wall. He did not ask you to do that, did he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask me to stay. Instead, he told me that I was free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you went back to the communications centre without having decoded the telegram?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge there were no other communicators at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, Mitar Lazarevic and the other person present were not able to decode telegrams because they would not have called you in the first place if they were able to decode. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not before I came -- or before the commander came. After that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know whether Sreten Acimovic was able to decode telegrams, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably when he sent me back to the communications centre he could have done that. I'm merely assuming. I don't know if he really did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because you don't know yourself whether the commander had the technical ability to decode telegrams?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: He pointed to the code table and said that that should -- document should be used to decode it, and then he sent me to the communications centre. I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mitar Lazarevic, when he testified he said that neither him or Sreten Acimovic were able to decode messages or telegrams. Can you confirm this information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't. How could I be able to confirm it when I wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's possible after you left that Sreten Acimovic could not decode this telegram?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of answer I should give you to that since I left and I wasn't able to know if he decoded it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you went back to the communications centre, no other communicators were sent to the battalion command for the purpose of decoding a telegram?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And according to the information you gave the Prosecution, 40 minutes later a second telegram arrived at the communications centre. Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 30-40 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But this message, you received it personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also said that you wrote it down into your normal book in the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, why would the second telegram be sent to the communications centre if the first message was sent directly to the battalion command? Was there any reason you can think of, technical reasons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was up to them to decide how they would be sending their telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, based on the information you gave to the Prosecution, you're not sure whether that second telegram was coded, but you know that part of the telegram said that the first telegram had to be sent to company commanders. That's what you told the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that it stated that the company commanders were supposed to be acquainted with the earlier telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this part that you identified, that part of was not coded, I take it. You didn't use Razgovornik to identify that part. That part, as a minimum, was not coded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was ordinary text, ordinary text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you communicated this message to the battalion command using the induction phone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, had this message -- this telegram been coded, you would have to say those numbers or coded words over the induction phone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, had this been the case, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't remember saying words and numbers to the battalion command on the phone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you asked me ten years ago, I might have been able to remember. It's been a while now. I saw that the coded part of it was already down at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, nothing happened until then until the induction phone rang again, and it -- you were asked to link up the battalion command with the company commanders. Is that what you recall, based on the information you provided to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you established that communication with the company commanders, but you did not stay on the line to listen to what was being said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I established communication with the commands of the companies, and I did not stay there to listen to what their conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I refer to your interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to have in e-court, and that's 3D00567, and I'd like to have, it's page 5 in English and in B/C/S page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, I would like to read what you said in your interview. And I will quote from lines 28 on page 4, until line 7 on page 5. And in English it goes as follows: "Okay. Regarding the second telegram --" this is question by Tomasz Blaszczyk. "Okay, regarding the second telegram, there was information that the company commanders had to be noticed about the previous telegram." Your answer was: "Yes." "Q. Did you inform the company commanders as the head of the communication of the battalion? "A. No. "Q. Do you know who informed them? "A. No. "Q. Did they come to the battalion headquarters shortly after? "A. I did not see, and I cannot claim in which way they were informed, or if they were informed." Can you read this in your language?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, you, yourself, did not transmit neither the first nor the second telegram to the companies, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am sure about the first one; I'm sure that I didn't. And as for the second, whether I transmitted the coded part or not, I can't remember it because the commander asked to be put through and to speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you, yourself, personally did not transmit any information to the companies, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. When it was decoded, I'm sure that I didn't. Whether I transmitted the coded part or not, I really can't remember. At one point the commander asked for the company commanders to be informed, and then he wanted to talk to them personally. I don't know whether I sent it or not. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you're not aware of any company commanders coming to the battalion command that night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have in e-court, please, 3D00566.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I refer you to paragraph 5 of this information report. This is information provided to the Defence by the Prosecution, information that would have been obtained by you the day after your interview. And at paragraph 5 it reads as follows: "At one moment during our conversation, Stevanovic suddenly referred to yesterday's interview (3rd of February 2009) and said that he thinks that he was ordered to send the second telegram (with the notice to inform the company commanders) to the company commanders also with the coded message from the previous telegram." Now, sir, this appears to be different from what you just mentioned. Can you explain this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you, the commander ordered - and I can't be sure of that - that the coded part should be sent to the company commanders. I don't know whether I did that or not because he spoke to them directly, immediately thereafter. And this is the whole -- what the whole thing is about. I can't be sure that I ever sent that. I believe that I had received the order to send the coded part to the company commanders. But then the company commanders decided to speak to them directly. He decided that immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, I move to a different topic. And can you confirm that to your knowledge, the 2nd Battalion never sent any telegrams to the Zvornik Brigade command during the time you were a member of the 2nd Battalion command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the coded telegrams or telegrams in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In general, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't confirm that. The telegrams were sent from both sides, but less from the battalion command to the brigade command. More often, telegrams arrived from the brigade command to the battalion commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, the night that you say a coded telegram would have been received, as you say, before 13 July, can you confirm that to your recollection no telegram were sent to the Zvornik Brigade through the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to a different topic, sir, and that is your knowledge concerning the capability of other communicators to code or decode messages. You mention today in your response that you said Ilic could decode messages. Is this something -- did you ever see Ilic code or decode a message before your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ilic was my mentor because he had become a signalsman before me. That's why I said it. He taught me some of the things that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you never saw him code or decode any messages while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. There may have been such occasions. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we talk about Cvijetinovic, you don't know whether he was able or not able to decode messages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know about him. I did not see him engaged in either coding or the decoding of the messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you ever tell specifically to Cvijetinovic, By the way, the Razgovornik is in the drawer. Did you ever tell him something like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why would I have told him that? It was a notorious fact, it was a document that we were all aware of. We were all aware of its existence. He knew it. We all had to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, you never saw him with the Razgovornik in his hands, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say that I did or that I didn't. How should I know what people were holding in their hands 15 years ago. You have to appreciate that, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I do, sir. However, the -- my question is, when we talk about Cvijetinovic, he testified in this case when he was asked whether you could code or decode messages, he said, "I say no." Those were his specific words. Is it possible that he did not know that you were able to code or decode messages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that he didn't know that I knew? Is that what you asked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what to answer you. I had carried a RUP, I had already coded telegrams in the field. Whether he was aware of that or not, I really wouldn't know. I don't know whether he knew that. I don't know how well abreast he was of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just with respect to receiving the Razgovornik, would you agree that, first of all, it was maintained in the communications centre because it was used, if any, for radio communications? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did anyone have to sign? If you receive a Razgovornik and it contains codes, I would imagine someone would have to sign for this, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody ever signed anything. At least I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how was it transmitted from the brigade to the battalion? Because you can confirm that there is no teleprinter. You can only receive documents physically; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, somebody did bring them, either couriers or whoever went to the brigade, and then they would bring them down to the command and where -- that's where we would take them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So there were -- there were no procedures when a new table was received in terms of telling everybody, Hey, guys, by the way we received a new Razgovornik. There was no procedure like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were always issued a couple of days before they were to be changed. This would be announced. It was always a couple of days before the end of the month, an announcement would come as to the date, when and -- the new Razgovornik would become operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you did not, yourself, as the commander of the communications centre, inform specifically the members of your section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to new Razgovornik documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they would inform me; for example, if I was at home and in the meantime a new document arrived, they would tell me that it had arrived, and I would know exactly where to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have about no more than ten minutes. If I can have the break now to look at my notes, I will save some time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. May I ask the remaining Defence teams if anyone wishes to cross-examine this witness? Ms. Fauveau, negative; Mr. Haynes, negative; Mr. Josse, negative. You are not thinking of any re-examination, I suppose, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss that with Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We need to finish this witness today, just keep that in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have very few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, sir, and we'll be done. Sir, about the second telegram which was received, Sretan Acimovic testified - and that was on page 13129-13130 - that in the telegram that he says was received on the 14th of July in the night, it was emphasized to respond by the same means, by coded telegram. Now, my question is the following: The second telegram, the one that you say you received before 13 July, you recall that part of it was the information should be transmitted to company commanders. Do you recall any information to the effect that a response should be sent by coded telegram to whoever had sent -- you had sent the telegram to the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if Sretan Acimovic says that the telegram he received, it was emphasized to respond by the same means by coded telegram, once again we can't be talking about the same telegram. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the telegram I received didn't contain that. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your interview, and I quote now from the last page of your interview, I won't put it up on the e-court. But that was the last page, lines 1-4, after the investigator Tomasz Blaszczyk said thank you. You added: "And I really don't remember who signed these telegrams or the exact time when they arrived." Can you recall that you said this during your interview, and can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And of course when we talk about who signed these telegrams, we are not talking about a signature, are we?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know either the function of the signing person or his first or last name. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is for both the first and the second telegram?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One thing we discuss concerning the use of codes -- and you confirm that codes were rarely used even for radio communication. Now, what I would like to -- maybe I can avoid showing it on e-court, but we have admitted in this case a long series of tactical intercepts. Those are radio communications within the Zvornik Brigade that were intercepted by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If I suggest to you that within these tactical intercepts that we have no codes are used, would you be surprised with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Also with respect to the testimony of Sretan Acimovic, there is something that he mentioned during one of the interviews that was communicated to us by the Prosecution which was not covered during his testimony. And I will quote from the -- his interview of 17 March, 2002, at page 10-11. And he said the following: "Since this concerns written or printed telegram, there was -- there is a possibility that somebody outside from the Zvornik Brigade might have used the operations officer because the duty operations officer had to receive orders and to transmit telegrams as they were ordered. So they might have been used for these purposes by somebody outside the Zvornik Brigade." Now, my question to you is the following: The coded telegram you say was received at the 2nd Battalion command before 13 July 1995, do you know where it came from? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My second question is, if it came from the Zvornik Brigade, is it possible that somebody outside, another agency outside of the Zvornik Brigade had the information transit through the Zvornik Brigade and then to the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. I can't assess the possibility at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: From a technical perspective, somebody, for example in another municipality, could call the Zvornik Brigade switchboard and relay a telegram to the 2nd Battalion. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I fully understood your question. They could dial the in-house switchboard or the brigade switchboard. Which are you referring to, to the brigade switchboard and to convey the telegram to the 2nd Battalion? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I may be more clear. Someone is in a municipality other than Zvornik and they wished to send a coded telegram to the 2nd Battalion. In order to do so, they would have to call the switchboard in the Zvornik Brigade and then be connected to the 2nd Battalion. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That should be the standard procedure, but one can use a civilian phone to call from Holland or Australia or wherever.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the procedure at the higher level of the command was is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, we have as your answer here: "That should be the standard procedure, but one can use a civilian phone to call from Holland or Australia or wherever," and then you said something else. Do you remember what you said? Because the interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One can use civilian phone lines to call the 2nd Battalion command from wherever. To what extent the document is relevant for the 2nd Battalion command is quite a different matter, if it does not go via the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, to your recollection, the telegram you say would have been received by the 2nd Battalion before the 13 July 1995, did both telegrams originate from the same source? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then I will move on. The only possibility other than to send the telegram by a courier to the company commanders, you will agree with me, would be to transmit that through the induction phone. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: A telegram from where for the company commanders? From the brigade or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, from the 2nd Battalion, from the command, and you want to send a telegram to the company commanders. So my first question is, did you ever do that? Or you just transmitted the information orally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The information was transmitted sometimes orally, sometimes in writing. It depended on the situation. Sometimes the battalion commander would write a telegram, and it would then be forwarded to company commanders. At other times they would speak to each other, so it would be done orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that if the 2nd Battalion command wants to send information to the company commanders, the only way it can be done is by using the induction phone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to make sure it's safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when Sretan Acimovic testified - and I refer to page 12948 - he said: "I got in touch with the company commanders, and I asked them if they had received the telegram. I think I asked them if they had received a telegram, and they confirmed that, yes, they had." Now, based on your testimony, did Sretan Acimovic call the company commanders more than once to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I object to the question because my friend hasn't established a basis of knowledge for the witness to answer it. He's in a completely different building according to the record of his testimony thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can make it more clear, Mr. President. I don't see the objection, but I can make it more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sure you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You testified to this, sir, that at some point you received a phone call from the battalion command while you were sitting in the communications centre. Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this was after the second telegram was received and that you had communicated its content to the battalion command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did Sretan Acimovic call you in the communications centre at any other time that night to be plugged in to the companies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Perhaps it wasn't Sretan Acimovic himself but the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the same night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But to your knowledge you, in the communications centre, before Sretan Acimovic called you, we established which he called you, do you have any knowledge of those telegrams or the telegram being sent to the company commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge as to the period before his call, and I said that I can't recall exactly whether I first sent the coded part to the lines or not, and whether it was only then that the commander took over the line and talked to company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, the -- the two telegrams that you say were received by the 2nd Battalion before the 13th of July, 1995. Would you agree with me that you never discussed these telegrams with anybody else after that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would there have been a reason based on your professional competence to inform the other communicators about such a telegram?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I spent some time in the office after that. And thereafter everything seems to have been forgotten. Nobody ever spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, it's just because in your interview you stated at one point when you were asked whether you remember receiving the telegram by yourself, you said "I don't remember, but I knew for sure that none of my colleagues knew about this telegram." So I'm just saying that you did not discuss this telegram that you received that night with your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it that it's, yes, you did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's true, I did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mention earlier in your testimony that the coded telegram that was handed to you when you arrive at the battalion command was on an A4 sheet of paper, that you never saw this telegram in a notebook. My question is the following: If Mitar Lazarevic testified that the telegram he received on 14 July was recorded in a notebook, then this again would confirm that we are not talking about the same telegram. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can only agree that this was on a piece of paper, A4. I don't know where the second telegram was recorded. Maybe it was subsequently recorded in the book of telegrams at the command. I suppose it was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, would you agree with me that throughout the time you spent with the 2nd Battalion, the only time you ever saw a telegram using codes other than something transmitted by radio was that night before the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you sir, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I confirm that none of the over Defence teams wishes to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Vanderpuye, leave us about five minutes or a little bit more towards the end, because we need them to make some new communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, good afternoon to Your Honours, good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Stevanovic. I have just a few questions for you. Let me start by picking up where my colleague left off. In his last question to you, he asked you if the only time you ever saw a telegram using codes other than something transmitted over the radio was the night before 13th of July. Your answer was "Yes." Did you discuss with any of your colleagues any coded telegram that was received in July of 1995 at any time prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did you discuss this coded telegram with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe two or these years ago. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have in e-court please 3D00565 in e-court, please. If we could go to page 2, please. It's the last paragraph, paragraph 11. And if we could blow it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to read to you a section of your interview with Mr. Blaszczyk on 24 September, 2008. And it reads as follows, this paragraph: "About a year ago a few colleagues of Stevanovic approached him and asked him whether he remembers or whether he had received any coded telegram from the brigade regarding the prisoners kept in the Rocevic school. Stevanovic said he had no knowledge about it. He did not want to disclose to me the name of his colleagues who had asked him about this." First of all, do you recall having this conversation with Mr. Blaszczyk on 24th September, 2008?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware whether Mitar Lazarevic or Sreco Acimovic testified in this case concerning the telegram that my colleague has put to you on cross-examination, the two telegrams?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that from Mr. Tomasz Blaszczyk, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You never heard that prior to that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in Montenegro, I wasn't there. I did hear some things, but I never discussed that with anybody. And, no, I did not hear about that before. Tomasz Blaszczyk told me that at our first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You never heard that from any other colleague, anybody where you live, prior till your discussion with Mr. Blaszczyk; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were rumors in the village, but I really can't tell you this or that person told me so-and-so. I heard about Sreco but not about Mitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when your colleagues asked you about whether or not you had any information about a coded telegram from the brigade regarding prisoners in the school, it's fair to say you never mentioned to them at all that you ever received any coded telegram at all in July of 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. That means your testimony ends here, and you are free to go back home. Our staff will assist you. Before you leave this courtroom, however, I wish to thank you for having come over and wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. 4467, 65 ter 4467, if my colleague is not planning to tender 3D00565, I would like to tender that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I've lost track of the numbers, so I don't know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no documents to tender, Mr. President, and I would oppose that because I quoted -- every single part that I wanted is quoted in the recorded. So there is no use to enter these documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Which document is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is the last one that I referred to. It is the interview with Mr. Stevanovic, dated 26, 2008. And the interview itself is 24 September 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if part of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That this document was not used by you, it was only used by Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's true, Mr. President. And I allowed the question. I should have basically said that it was not part of cross-examination, but the topic was a bit related, so I let that go through, then the Chamber ruled against me. But I don't see the reason to enter any of these documents. The relevant passages were quoted on the record, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, the document in question relates to -- directly to this witness's knowledge of the coded telegrams which are the subject -- which are at issue in this case, directly to that, which was the subject of cross-examination beyond any question. The specific issue that was put to him is in paragraph 11; that's true. The document itself, however, puts in context a couple of different things. And I think my colleague is well aware of them. One of them has to do with -- if we can go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session. Hold it, hold it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible to know if we will have a hearing next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm -- again I offer you my apologies. If there has been a lapse in the communication channel. We were informed that one or more of you had asked for a confirmation that there will not be any sittings, unannounced sittings, between now and the 21st of April when we start with the testimony of Momir Nikolic. It is not our intention to have any sittings unless there is a catastrophe which is provoked which would make it necessary to have a sitting, but I hope there will not be.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
